messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 63‑year‑old rabbi who has spent the last three decades guiding his community through prayers and sermons, came to the United States after fleeing the chaos of a war‑torn Balkan town in his twenties. That night, as he hurried through a narrow, dimly lit alley to escape a sudden gunfire, a rough hand brushed his shoulder—an unexpected touch—while the sight of a glinting weapon and the guttural shout of a militant filled the air. The shock of that moment still reverberates in his mind, and the memory of the stranger’s grip and the echo of the shout keep his senses on high alert. When a sudden touch or a sudden shout intrudes upon his day, David’s first response is to tell himself that he must be punished for surviving what he endured. This punishment thinking becomes a self‑imposed reproach that he repeats whenever the memory surfaces. At the same time, the tactile and auditory cues trigger his belief that his body is perpetually an enemy, reacting as if danger is imminent even in the quiet of his own home. Thus, the triggers of unexpected touch, visual weapons, and shouting drive both his maladaptive strategy of punishment thinking and his negative appraisal that his body is always on guard. The weight of these negative appraisals bears heavily on David’s sense of threat. He can no longer focus on the words of the Torah during services; his concentration slips, and he is constantly scanning the sanctuary for places that feel protected. He has begun to sit only in the front rows where a solid wall gives him a false sense of security, and he has stopped visiting the back pews that once felt welcoming. Because he believes he cannot rely on himself and that others would have stopped the attack, his perception of threat magnifies. This heightened threat, in turn, makes him more aware of the same triggers—every light touch, every distant shout feels like a sign that the past has returned. The growing sense of threat amplifies his maladaptive strategies. Whenever the feeling of danger creeps in, David retorts with self‑blame, telling himself that he deserves the suffering he has carried. He distracts himself by immersing in scripture, pulling his mind away from the possibility that a weapon could reappear or a shout could cut through his calm. He also steers clear of intimacy with his wife, fearing that closeness would expose the raw wounds he has hidden. The threat of danger not only reinforces his negative beliefs—that he cannot trust himself, that he is destined for suffering—but also makes him even more sensitive to the triggers he once tolerated. Over the years, the avoidance of intimacy and the constant self‑punishment have tightened a loop of pain. By refusing to share his memories with his partner, David has created a silence that feels as sharp as a weapon. His conviction that he must endure suffering feeds the shame that keeps him at arm’s length from emotional closeness. Each unexpected touch or distant shout he interprets as a reminder of that night, and his avoidance of close contact only deepens the isolation that feeds his fear. The cycle between his maladaptive strategies and his negative appraisals has made the triggers feel more imminent, and the triggers, in turn, reinforce his maladaptive coping. Today, David decided to seek help after an incident at the synagogue when a young congregant asked about his wartime experience. The question made his heart race, his body tense, and he felt the familiar wave of hypervigilance wash over him. He realized that his fear had begun to erode his ability to lead and to connect with his community. What has brought him here now is the fear that this relentless loop will one day consume his relationships entirely. He hopes to reclaim the sense of safety he once felt in the sanctuary, to restore the intimacy he shares with his wife, and to let go of the belief that the past will always claim them again.
